question: What is the maximum amount of annual leave most federal employees can carry over into the next leave year?
answer: The maximum amount of annual leave most federal employees can carry over into the next leave year is 240 hours, as specified in [5 U.S.C. 6304]. This applies to general schedule employees with less than 3 years of service.
gold_answer: 240 hours (30 days) [5 U.S.C. 6304(a)]

question: How much annual leave can a federal employee stationed overseas carry over?
answer: A federal employee stationed overseas can carry over a maximum of 45 days of annual leave into the next leave year, as specified in the OPM fact sheet on Annual Leave. This is outlined in the text: "[OPM fact sheet: Annual Leave > Annual Leave Ceilings] Annual Leave Ceilings... Federal Employees Stationed Overseas*; 45 days." [OPM fact sheet: Annual Leave > Annual Leave Ceilings]
gold_answer: 45 days (360 hours) [5 U.S.C. 6304(b)]

question: What is the annual leave carryover limit for Senior Executive Service members?
answer: The annual leave carryover limit for Senior Executive Service (SES) members is 90 days (720 hours) according to the OPM fact sheet on annual leave ceilings [OPM fact sheet: Annual Leave > Annual Leave Ceilings]. This limit applies to SES members, as well as Senior-Level and Scientific and Professional employees, and is higher than the standard 30 days for employees stationed within the United States.
gold_answer: 90 days (720 hours) [5 U.S.C. 6304(f)]

question: How fast does a full-time federal employee accrue sick leave?
answer: A full-time federal employee accrues sick leave at a rate of **one-half day (4 hours)** for each full biweekly pay period, as stated in the OPM fact sheet on sick leave entitlement [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave (General Information) > Sick Leave Entitlement]. This rate applies to most full-time employees, with exceptions for specific roles like members of the Firefighting Division of the Fire Department of the District of Columbia, who accrue two-fifths of a day (approximately 3.2 hours) per biweekly pay period [5 U.S.C. 6307(a)].
gold_answer: 4 hours (½ day) per biweekly pay period [5 U.S.C. 6307(a)]

question: Is there a cap on how much sick leave I can accumulate?
answer: There is no general limitation on the amount of sick leave that can be accumulated, as stated in the OPM fact sheet on sick leave accumulation [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave (General Information) > Sick Leave Accumulation]. However, specific provisions may apply depending on the situation, such as the use of sick leave for adoption or medical emergencies, which may have certain restrictions. For more detailed information, you may need to consult the specific regulations or contact your agency's HR department.
gold_answer: No, there is no limit on accumulated sick leave [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave (General Information)]

question: How many hours of sick leave can I use in a leave year for general family care or bereavement?
answer: You are entitled to use up to 13 days (104 hours) of sick leave each leave year for general family care or bereavement purposes. This is part of the broader entitlement of up to 12 weeks (480 hours) of sick leave to care for a family member with a serious health condition. If you have already used any portion of the 13 days for general family care or bereavement, that amount must be subtracted from the 12-week entitlement. You are also entitled to no more than a combined total of 12 weeks of sick leave each leave year for all family care purposes [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave to Care for a Family Member with a Serious Health Condition > Sick Leave Usage Limits Per Leave Year].
gold_answer: Up to 104 hours (13 days) per leave year [5 CFR 630.401(b)]

question: How much sick leave can I use to care for a family member with a serious health condition?
answer: You are entitled to use up to 12 weeks (480 hours) of sick leave each leave year to care for a family member with a serious health condition. This includes 13 days (104 hours) of sick leave for general family care or bereavement purposes. If you have already used any portion of the 13 days for general family care or bereavement, that amount must be subtracted from the 12-week entitlement. You are also entitled to no more than a combined total of 12 weeks of sick leave each leave year for all family care purposes [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave to Care for a Family Member with a Serious Health Condition > Sick Leave Usage Limits Per Leave Year].
gold_answer: Up to 480 hours (12 administrative workweeks) per leave year [5 CFR 630.401(c)]

question: How much FMLA leave is a federal employee entitled to?
answer: Federal employees are entitled to a total of up to 12 workweeks of unpaid FMLA leave during any 12-month period for specific purposes, such as the birth or placement of a child, care of a family member with a serious health condition, or qualifying exigencies related to a family member's covered active duty in the Armed Forces [5 U.S.C. 6382(a)(1)]. The 12-month period begins on the first day the employee uses FMLA leave and continues for 12 months from that date. Some categories of employees, such as those with intermittent schedules or temporary appointments, may be excluded from FMLA eligibility.
gold_answer: 12 administrative workweeks in any 12-month period [5 U.S.C. 6382(a)(1)]

question: How much paid parental leave can a federal employee take after the birth of a child?
answer: Federal employees are entitled to up to 12 weeks of Paid Parental Leave (PPL) in a 12-month period following the birth or placement of a child for adoption or foster care. This leave is available to each parent-employee separately, and there is no combined limit for married employees employed by the same agency. PPL is a type of paid leave that may substitute for unpaid FMLA leave. The entitlement to PPL expires at the end of the 12-month period beginning on the date of the birth or placement of the child. [OPM fact sheet: Paid Parental Leave > Married Employees Employed by Same Agency] [OPM fact sheet: Paid Parental Leave > Introduction]
gold_answer: 12 administrative workweeks of paid parental leave [5 U.S.C. 6382(d)(2)]

question: How many days of leave can I get to donate bone marrow?
answer: You are entitled to up to 7 days of paid leave each calendar year to serve as a bone marrow donor and up to 30 days of paid leave each calendar year to serve as an organ donor. These are separate from annual and sick leave. [5 U.S.C. 6327(b)]
gold_answer: Up to 7 days [5 U.S.C. 6327(b)(1)]

question: How much leave is available to a federal employee who donates an organ?
answer: A federal employee who donates an organ is entitled to up to 30 days of paid leave each calendar year for that purpose. This leave is in addition to annual and sick leave. The leave is provided under 5 U.S.C. 6327, which ensures that the employee does not lose pay or benefits for the time spent as an organ donor. The leave is available on an as-needed basis, and there is no carryover of unused days to the next calendar year.
gold_answer: Up to 30 days [5 U.S.C. 6327(b)(2)]

question: What is the maximum disabled veteran leave a new employee can be credited?
answer: The maximum disabled veteran leave a new employee can be credited is 104 hours. This is based on the Wounded Warriors Federal Leave Act of 2015, which entitles eligible employees to up to 104 hours of disabled veteran leave for the purposes of undergoing medical treatment for a service-connected disability. This leave is a one-time benefit provided to an eligible employee, and the employee will have a single, continuous 12-month eligibility period beginning on the "first day of employment" to use the leave or it will be forfeited [5 U.S.C. 6329(b)(1)].
gold_answer: Up to 104 hours [5 U.S.C. 6329(b)(1)]

question: What is the most sick leave an agency can advance to an employee?
answer: The maximum amount of sick leave an agency can advance to a full-time employee is 240 hours (30 days) at any one time. This applies to situations such as the employee's own illness, injury, pregnancy, childbirth, or exposure to a communicable disease, or for the care of a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness. For part-time employees, the maximum amount of advanced sick leave must be prorated according to the number of hours in their regularly scheduled administrative workweek [OPM fact sheet: Advanced Sick Leave > Maximum Amount of Advanced Sick Leave].
gold_answer: Up to 240 hours (30 days) [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave (General Information)]

question: Under the Emergency Leave Transfer Program, how much donated annual leave can one recipient receive at a time?
answer: The maximum amount of donated annual leave that an emergency leave recipient can receive at one time from an emergency leave transfer program is 240 hours for each disaster or emergency [5 CFR 630.1111].
gold_answer: Up to 240 hours per disaster or emergency at any one time [OPM fact sheet: Emergency Leave Transfer Program]

question: If I scheduled annual leave in advance but got sick and couldn't use it before the year ended, can it be restored?
answer: The policy documents indicate that annual leave scheduled in advance can be restored under specific conditions. If you were unable to use your scheduled annual leave due to sickness, the agency may restore it if the leave was scheduled in writing before the start of the third biweekly pay period prior to the end of the leave year. Additionally, if the sickness was prolonged and prevented you from using the leave, the agency may consider restoring it. However, if the leave was not scheduled in advance, restoration is limited to very specific circumstances, such as national emergencies or administrative errors. You should consult with your agency's HR department to determine if your situation qualifies for restoration.
gold_answer: Yes, annual leave lost because of sickness when scheduled in advance is restored [5 U.S.C. 6304(d)(1)(C)]

question: Do I get extra pay for regularly scheduled night work, and how much?
answer: You are entitled to **10 percent extra pay** for regularly scheduled work performed at night, as per the federal policy. This is known as **night pay** and is computed as a percentage of your rate of basic pay, including any applicable locality payment or special rate supplement. The night pay differential applies to work scheduled between the hours of 6 p.m. and 6 a.m., unless otherwise designated by your agency. This additional pay is in addition to any holiday premium pay, Sunday pay, or overtime pay you may receive. [5 U.S.C. 5545(a)]
gold_answer: Yes, a night differential of 10% of basic pay for regularly scheduled work between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. [5 CFR 550.121(a)]

question: What premium pay do I get for working on a Sunday as part of my regular schedule?
answer: You are entitled to Sunday premium pay equal to 25 percent of your rate of basic pay for each hour of Sunday work. Sunday work consists of nonovertime work during your regularly scheduled basic tour of duty (not to exceed 8 hours) that begins or ends on a Sunday. If you work on Sunday as part of your regular schedule, you will receive this premium pay for the hours worked on Sunday [OPM fact sheet: Sunday Premium Pay > Entitlement].
gold_answer: Basic pay plus 25% premium pay for each hour of Sunday work [5 CFR 550.171(a)]

question: For a non-exempt employee, at what rate is overtime paid under the FLSA and when does it start?
answer:
Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), non-exempt federal employees are entitled to overtime pay at a rate of one and one-half times their hourly regular rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of 8 hours in a day or 40 hours in a workweek [5 CFR 551.501(a)(4)]. 

The overtime pay is calculated by multiplying the employee's "straight time rate of pay" by all overtime hours worked, plus one-half of the employee's "hourly regular rate of pay" times all overtime hours worked. This calculation includes any applicable special rate supplements or locality payments in the "total remuneration" and "straight time rate of pay" [OPM fact sheet: How to Compute FLSA Overtime Pay > Background]. 

The overtime hours are determined based on the employee's work schedule and the specific overtime standard applicable to their position. For example, some positions may have a weekly overtime standard of 42.75 hours, resulting in 16.25 hours of overtime pay under the FLSA [OPM fact sheet: Guidance on Applying FLSA Overtime Provisions to Law Enforcement Employees Receiving Administratively Uncontrollable Overtime Pay > A. Overtime Hours]. 

This overtime pay is required for all overtime work that is ordered or approved, as well as for work that is "suffered or permitted," except for flexible schedule employees [OPM fact sheet: How to Compute FLSA Overtime Pay > Background].
gold_answer: 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 8 in a day or 40 in a workweek [5 CFR 551.501(a)]

question: How many hours is the basic workweek for a full-time federal employee?
answer: The basic workweek for a full-time federal employee is 40 hours, as established by 5 CFR 610.111. This workweek does not extend over more than 6 of any 7 consecutive days [5 CFR 610.111(a)(1)].
gold_answer: 40 hours, not over more than 6 of any 7 consecutive days [5 CFR 610.111(a)(1)]

question: How long do I need to have worked for the government before I can use FMLA leave?
answer: To be eligible for FMLA leave under OPM’s regulations, you must have completed **12 months of qualifying civilian or military service**. This requirement can be met through any combination of qualifying civilian service and qualifying military service, and the 12 months do not need to be consecutive or recent. Additionally, you must be covered by the title 5 leave system for annual and sick leave purposes and not be specifically excluded from eligibility. [OPM fact sheet: Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) 12-Week Entitlement > 12 Months of Qualifying Civilian or Military Service]
gold_answer: At least 12 months of service [5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(B)]

question: Can I take compensatory time off instead of being paid for irregular overtime?
answer:
You may be eligible to take compensatory time off (CTO) instead of being paid for irregular or occasional overtime work, but this depends on your employment status and the agency's policies. 

For **FLSA-exempt employees** whose basic pay is above the GS-10, step 10 rate, agencies may require CTO in lieu of overtime pay for irregular or occasional overtime work. However, this is not mandatory for wage employees or for FLSA overtime pay. 

For **non-exempt employees**, CTO may be approved at the request of the employee for irregular or occasional overtime work, but it is not required. Additionally, CTO may be approved for regularly scheduled overtime work under flexible work schedule programs. 

For more specific guidance, consult your agency's policies or contact your HR office.
gold_answer: Yes, at the employee's request the agency may grant compensatory time off instead of overtime pay [5 CFR 550.114(a)]

question: What is the maximum recruitment incentive as a share of annual basic pay?
answer:
The maximum recruitment incentive as a share of annual basic pay is generally limited to 25 percent of the employee's annual rate of basic pay at the beginning of the service period multiplied by the number of years (including fractions of a year) in the service period, as stated in [5 CFR 575.109(b)(1)].

However, there is a possibility of a waiver allowing up to 50 percent of the annual rate of basic pay, provided the agency determines a critical need, as outlined in [5 CFR 575.109(c)(1)]. This waiver is not applicable to all cases and requires specific documentation and justification.
gold_answer: Generally up to 25% of annual basic pay for the service period [5 CFR 575.109(b)(1)]

question: What is the maximum retention incentive an individual employee can be authorized?
answer: The maximum retention incentive an individual employee can be authorized is up to 50 percent of the employee's basic pay, as stated in 5 CFR 575.309(e)(1). This is subject to a waiver request and approval by an authorized agency official, based on critical agency needs and the employee's unique qualifications. Under normal circumstances, the maximum retention incentive for an individual employee is 25 percent of the employee's basic pay, as specified in 5 CFR 575.309(a)(1).
gold_answer: 25% of basic pay for an individual employee [5 CFR 575.309(a)(1)]

question: I'm at GS step 2. How long must I wait for my next within-grade increase?
answer: The waiting period for a within-grade increase (WGI) depends on your current step. For a GS employee at step 2, the waiting period to advance to step 3 is 52 weeks of creditable service in step 2. This is outlined in the OPM fact sheet on within-grade increases [OPM fact sheet: Within-Grade Increases > Required Waiting Periods]. If you have received a quality step increase (QSI) that places you in a higher step, the waiting period for the next step increase will be adjusted accordingly, as explained in the OPM fact sheet on QSI timing [OPM fact sheet: Quality Step Increase > Timing Matters].
gold_answer: 52 calendar weeks of creditable service (steps 1–3) [5 CFR 531.405(a)]

question: How long is the waiting period between step 5 and step 6?
answer: The waiting period between step 5 and step 6 is 104 weeks of creditable service in step 5 [OPM fact sheet: Within-Grade Increases > Required Waiting Periods]. The waiting period for advancement from step 6 to step 7 is also 104 weeks, and from step 7 to step 8, it is 156 weeks.
gold_answer: 104 calendar weeks (steps 4–6) [5 CFR 531.405(a)]

question: How long is the wait for a within-grade increase once I'm at step 7 or above?
answer: The waiting period for a within-grade increase from step 7 to step 8 is 156 calendar weeks of creditable service in step 7. Similarly, the waiting period for advancement from step 8 to step 9 is also 156 calendar weeks of creditable service in step 8. This is specified in the OPM fact sheet on Within-Grade Increases and corroborated by 5 CFR 531.405. The waiting period begins on the first appointment as an employee of the Federal Government or on receiving an equivalent increase.
gold_answer: 156 calendar weeks [5 CFR 531.405(a)(iii)]

question: What is the most administrative leave an agency can place an employee on in a calendar year?
answer: The most administrative leave an agency can place an employee on in a calendar year is 10 workdays, as specified in 5 U.S.C. 6329a(b)(1) and 5 CFR 630.1404. This limit applies specifically to administrative leave for investigative purposes. If an employee reaches this 10-workday limit, the agency may then use investigative leave provisions under 5 U.S.C. 6329b for continued investigations. This limit is separate for each agency that employs the employee during the year.
gold_answer: No more than 10 work days per calendar year [5 U.S.C. 6329a(b)(1)]

question: When does the federal leave year begin?
answer: The federal leave year begins on the first day of the first full biweekly pay period in a calendar year and ends on the day immediately before the first day of the first full biweekly pay period in the following calendar year [OPM fact sheet: Annual Leave > Leave Year Beginning and Ending Dates]. Employees may carry over a maximum amount of accrued annual leave (240 hours for most employees) into the next leave year.
gold_answer: On the first day of the first full biweekly pay period in the calendar year [OPM fact sheet: Leave Year]

question: If my office closes for a snowstorm, can my agency give me paid leave?
answer: Under 5 U.S.C. 6329c, an agency may approve the provision of paid leave to an employee or group of employees due to weather or safety issues, such as a snowstorm, if the employee is prevented from safely traveling to or performing work at an approved location. This leave is available specifically when the cause is an act of God, a terrorist attack, or other applicable conditions. The agency is not required to provide this leave but may do so without loss of pay or credit for time or service. If the closure results in an employee being unable to reschedule and use "use or lose" annual leave before the end of the leave year, the leave may be forfeited. For specific guidance on your situation, consult your agency's HR department.
gold_answer: Yes, weather and safety leave without loss of pay may be approved [5 U.S.C. 6329c(b)]

question: Do I have to agree to keep working for my agency after taking paid parental leave?
answer: Yes, you are required to agree to work for your agency for not less than 12 weeks beginning on your first scheduled workday after your paid parental leave concludes. This agreement must be in writing, and it can be a handwritten signature, an electronic signature, or documented in an email or text message, provided you supply the required signature within 24 hours [5 CFR 630.1705(a) and (b)]. The agreement applies regardless of the actual amount of leave you use [OPM fact sheet: Paid Parental Leave > Advanced Written Service Agreement].
gold_answer: Yes, you must agree in writing beforehand to work for the agency for at least 12 weeks after the leave ends [5 U.S.C. 6382(d)(2)]

question: Is there a minimum length of service to be eligible for paid parental leave?
answer: The minimum length of service required to be eligible for paid parental leave (PPL) is 12 months of service as an employee, within the meaning of section 6381(1)(A) of title 5 U.S.C. This requirement applies before the date of the applicable birth or placement involved. Additionally, an employee must meet all eligibility requirements for use of Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave to be eligible for PPL. Employees with temporary appointments, intermittent work schedules, or fewer than 12 months of qualifying federal service are not eligible for FMLA leave and thus are not eligible for PPL. [5 U.S.C. 6382(d)(2)(iii)(E)]
gold_answer: Yes, at least 12 months of service before the birth or placement [5 U.S.C. 6382(d)(2)]
